National Assembly
Assembly of the People
21st Session
Details of Proceedings
Complete
13 Jestha 2083
Wednesday
Meeting
Number - 1
The National Assembly's meeting today commenced at 13:19 hours under the chairmanship of the Right Honourable Chairperson Mr. Narayan Prasad Dahal.
Right Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Members,
(13:19 hrs)
The proceedings commence.
Honourable Members, names of Honourable Members have been presented to speak during Zero Hour. Each Honourable Member will be provided with 1 minute of time to speak during Zero Hour.
First, Honourable Member Chandra Bahadur KC.
Honourable Mr. Chandrabahadur KC (Nepali Congress): Honourable Chairperson,
(13:19 hrs)
In Nepal, 16 districts are currently affected by wildlife. Gulmi, Arghakhanchi, Dhankuta, and other 16 districts of Nepal are affected. A proposal has been prepared for a solar fence system called "Reliable Crop Protection Against Wildlife Threats" for this purpose. Therefore, I wish to present this proposal to the Honourable Chairperson to submit it to the ministry. Thank you. Jai Nepal.
Right Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Jagat Timilsina.
(13:20 hrs)
Honourable Mr. Jagat Timilsina (Nepali Congress): Honourable Chairperson,
(13:20 hrs)
Professors and staff who joined Tribhuvan University after 2065 have been protesting for 45 days now, an indefinite protest program. At a time when professors should be involved in incubation and innovative activities, and in research, they are protesting. Neither the government nor the concerned body has shown any interest in this. Today, through the Chairperson of this esteemed assembly, I wish to draw the government's attention to this matter. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Ranjit Karna.
(12:21 hrs)
Honourable Mr. Ranjit Karna (Nepali Congress): Honourable Chairperson,
(13:21 hrs)
The Health Insurance Board has suspended the health insurance program from private health institutions starting from Jestha 16th. I demand that this be immediately revoked. Furthermore, due to natural disasters that occur every year, there are significant losses of life and property. Especially since more than 60 percent of the affected areas are rural, with floods causing 40 percent of the damage, landslides 10 percent, and fires, I demand that rural settlements be managed scientifically. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Rekha Kumari Jha.
(12:22 hrs)
Honourable Ms. Rekha Kumari Jha (Nepal Communist Party, UML): Honourable Chairperson,
(13:22 hrs)
Reports are coming in that crimes related to theft, robbery, and drug trafficking have increased in some districts of the Terai region at this time. According to Nepal Police records, people have been apprehended with drugs in Jhapa, Parsa, and Banke districts. Smuggling and theft incidents are increasing along the border. This is due to idleness and unemployment, leading to armed robbery for money. Why is our administration remaining silent? Strict action must be taken against drug trafficking. Surveillance must be increased at the border. The youth must be provided with vocational training and employment programs. I wish to draw the attention of the Chairperson to issues such as engaging them in positive activities like sports. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Roshi Mechhe.
(13:23 hrs)
Honourable Mr. Roshi Mechhe (Nepal Communist Party, UML): Honourable Chairperson,
(13:23 hrs)
The federal government is repeatedly issuing directives to local levels to remove squatters and unmanaged settlements. But, ironically, there is neither alternative land nor shelter for their long-term management. I express my regret over such immature behaviour shown by the federal government. Chairperson, Article 37 of the Constitution of Nepal establishes the right to housing as a fundamental right. Is it the spirit of the constitution to throw citizens onto the streets without alternatives? Providing only removal without resources, means, and alternatives to local governments is merely shirking responsibility. I draw the serious attention of the government through the Chairperson. First, concrete alternatives and housing security should be ensured for squatters across the country. This undemocratic and unconstitutional act of displacing citizens without proper management should be stopped immediately. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Samjhana Devkota.
(13:24 hrs)
Honourable Ms. Samjhana Devkota (Nepal Communist Party, UML): Honourable Chairperson,
(13:25 hrs)
You repeatedly regulate Zero Hour and Special Time while the session is ongoing. Honourable members express their views here. However, the government has never responded to the queries raised during Zero Hour and Special Time. We always return unanswered. We always return without answers. Does this government not value this assembly, or has it failed to gather that information? If we do not receive appropriate responses from the government to the issues raised during Zero Hour and Special Time from now on, then Zero Hour and Special Time will have no significance. I wish to draw the attention of the Honourable Chairperson to this matter. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Somnath Poudel.
(13:25 hrs)
Honourable Mr. Somnath Poudel (Nepal Communist Party, UML):
(13:26 hrs)
Honourable Chairperson, on Baishakh 11, 2083, banana cultivation suffered significant damage due to storms in eastern Nepal. Banana crops planted on 60 bighas of land in Baradashi-7, Jhapa, and 12 bighas in Kamatoli, Jhapa Rural Municipality-3, were destroyed. This has caused a loss of approximately 35 million rupees to the farmers. The responsibility for insurance was given to Nepal Insurance Company in Jhapa. This insurance company has not insured the banana crops under various pretexts. Therefore, I demand that immediate action be taken against the insurance company that is not providing insurance under pretext. I also draw the attention of the Government of Nepal to provide necessary relief to the affected farmers. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Members, the turn for Honourable Members to speak during Zero Hour concludes here.
Honourable Members, names of Honourable Members have been presented on a party basis to speak during Special Time. Now, I will provide time for Honourable Members to speak. First, Honourable Member Kamala Panta, time 14 minutes. Following this, Honourable Member Rajendra Lakshmi Gaire.
Honourable Ms. Kamala Panta (Nepali Congress): Honourable Chairperson, I have some questions. My first question is about the Prime Minister's disregard for the parliament. Parliament is not just any parliament, Mr. Chairperson. Parliament is a practice in the world, and especially, the parliament of 2072, the Constituent Assembly, created our constitution. The key individuals who worked hard to create the constitution are here with us, in this house. The people have given rights through the constitution. This parliament forms the government. If the government formed by the parliament disregards the parliament itself, what will be the state of the parliament? Why is this disregard happening? And this party, that related party, the party that makes the Prime Minister, and the Prime Minister himself should be sensitive not about who came and who went. We don't care who becomes the Prime Minister. But the Prime Minister is an institution. If that institution is weakened, being disrespectful to the parliament that made you Prime Minister is a shameful act. Honourable Chairperson, I have considered sensitive issues for this party, that party, and especially the members of that party, and the Prime Minister's character of disregarding this parliament needs to be corrected. That is my first question. Next, regarding the President himself coming and attending an event, the person he appointed. Come to the parliament, this esteemed institution. I am not raising the issue of Ram Chandra Paudel as an individual. But the person invited to read the policy and program. Disrespecting a guest is not our character. It is not our tradition either. Why is this tradition being challenged now? We want to know the reason. I will talk about the next question. Instead of lobbying for their own policy and programs and presenting them well, leaving the assembly and disrespecting the assembly is a strange situation we have witnessed. I hope this does not happen again, and I wish that it does not happen again. Next question, we MPs have raised many issues. As Honourable members have said, we need answers from the government. What is happening where? What is the situation? Floods and landslides have occurred, disasters have struck. How many people were affected, or what is the situation? The member does not know. The member has been given the Council of Ministers. Accountability should be with them. When has he ever come forward proactively saying I will answer? The Chairperson should also regulate. The government should be told to answer. I see shortcomings in these matters. The government, this is our democracy. It has reached this point after great struggle. These old parties, they are called old parties. If these old parties had not brought us this far, where would we be? Would the current government have been formed? We must also look back. This is the rule of law. We have struggled so much for the rule of law, the rule of law. We are very happy now. The constitution, our current constitutional system. Doesn't that system mean majority rule? We thought this constitution itself was wrong. A single party has secured a two-thirds majority, we are happy. But it too must proceed constitutionally, uphold the rule of law. A party went to elections with a 100-point program, supposedly to win the election. Can that be implemented everywhere against the law? It is being implemented on employees, on students. Can it be implemented everywhere? One must think from the heart. Those in government, the ministers must think. We did not say that out of impulse. We want the rule of law. Will the programs that were put forward during the election establish the rule of law? These things must be considered. Next, the issue of squatters, Honourable members have raised it, I will not repeat it much. Where is the right to housing for the people? It is a fundamental right, the right to housing. Do they demolish houses first after managing everything, or do they demolish houses first and then manage everything, leaving the people stranded? What do they say? Those in power, think from your heart. Do you arrest first or provide shelter first? Pay some attention to that. Arrest first or shelter first. The private sector is distressed, capital is fleeing abroad, capital is fleeing. Is the government paying attention to how much capital is fleeing? We bring capital and do many miracles, build the country, provide employment. How?

Will employment come? Capital must be brought in. Our own capital is currently fleeing. The ministers, including myself, must evaluate this situation. The Prime Minister is only leading the government. The ministers are also responsible here. In a democracy, I find it strange that the government... I have been in parliament for many years. Does the government coordinate with the parties? Does it fight with them, ignore them, or engage in dialogue? I haven't had any dialogue with any party since this government came into power. We are also accountable to the public. We have also taken responsibility for what to do for the public. This is not just for the parties in the current government. But what is the sentiment? Dialogue is needed regarding the sentiment. It is not enough to just show the arrogance of the majority. The majority does nothing. We have also brought the majority many times, we have to think. Doesn't it say 'Wisdom arises from debate'? Discussion is needed, debate is needed, all parties must sit together. How many parties do we have? All parties must sit together. Stakeholders too. Has the government sat with the parties until today? We will not get anywhere by neglecting them. The government should consider this. Also, this government is anti-poor. I feel so. How much has the price of essentials increased? Is the hearth burning in the people's homes or not? We must look. Remember our ancestors. This is a country where our ancestors used to go to the roof to see if the hearth was burning in the people's homes. Does the government go anywhere by neglecting the people, causing them suffering, killing farmers, and letting the poor die? The poor must be encouraged, put to work, given work. Are they fed or not? The government must ask the public, 'Are you fed?' Does it have any such policy? That 100-day program is just a program for the election. It is not a systematic matter. We can choose not to accept it. All employees are terrified, no one speaks. Is this how governance works? The fare for public transport has increased three times. How difficult it is for people to travel, has anyone considered it? Has the government paid attention to such matters? Farmers are not getting the price for their produce. We are consumers. We consume milk every day by paying the price. We have paid the price. But the farmers are not getting the money for the milk, where did it go? Such things should be investigated. Chasing which party went where and whom to blame is useless. The price of milk must be paid immediately. Farmers are not selling tomatoes now. They say they haven't got the price for potatoes. Why haven't they? Farmers work hard to produce. If the government wants to be popular with the produce, the budget is coming soon, the government should say, 'Public, you increase production, I will buy even a single cabbage,' and show courage. That would be courage. Just causing suffering to the public everywhere will achieve nothing. Nepal's most important crop is paddy. It's time to plant paddy. There is a problem with fertilizer. And the government has already said that farmers will get even less fertilizer this year than last year. So how will farmers cultivate? Farmers don't have to cultivate. How will fertilizer come? What is its alternative source? Alternative sources must be provided. Where is that source? What is that alternative source? And now the paddy planting season has arrived, there is no fertilizer. And if vegetables are produced, there is no price. Imports are coming from abroad, exports are stopped. There is a trade deficit. How much attention has been paid to these issues? The public came with the promise that we will work for the farmers on these very issues. I heard, I am also from the hills. When asking for votes, I was also in the village. We also went to ask for votes. The parties in the current government also went to ask for votes. There is a monkey menace. In the hills, no one can live. Either there are tigers, wild boars, or monkeys, they eat their crops, they cannot cultivate anywhere. Tigers are causing so much trouble now. If someone raises buffaloes, they fear they will be killed any day. Tigers have entered goat sheds. Such things are small matters but become big. Honorable Chairperson, the ministers of the government must be told. Chairperson, you must rule. How is the monkey problem being solved? Every day, MPs here are raising the monkey problem. The problem of tigers and wild animals. What is the program? Is the program only to drive people away, or is it a program to only trouble the poor? Does the government actually have any relief programs? Attention must also be paid to those programs. Also, in the government's 100-day program, at number 75, it is said that the Drinking Water Corporation will be abolished. After abolishing the Drinking Water Corporation, what is the alternative solution? In the Madhesh region, from east to west, in that entire area, about 500 projects... we talk about water, what do we say? Drinking water, sanitation, cleanliness. Four hundred are in disarray, some are ongoing. All these are drinking water projects through the corporation. Tomorrow, the government will say to the public, 'Wait, I will close your water source and you will drink water later, like demolishing a house.' Is that it? That's it, isn't it? Abolishing the Drinking Water Corporation now means saying, 'We will close the water source now and give you water later.' Management must be done first, everything must be organized. Only then is the process. It's five years, isn't it? If the government is going to run for only a few months and say we can't do it, then we have nothing to say. The mandate given by the public is for five years, so why the hurry, why the panic? Work can be done slowly. If the government had first told the landless, 'Build your houses and then live,' and then demolished them, who would have said anything to the government? We have spoken wrongly. If the government has made a mistake, let it say so. Our Prime Minister, who made a mistake himself, cannot even answer other MPs. Also, the current panic among employees. Trade unions, this is a constitutional right. The right given by the constitution must be abolished, or the constitution must be amended by a two-thirds majority. Let the 100-point agenda be passed by amending the constitution, we have nothing to say. But if it is constitutional, then work must be done according to the constitution. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson - Honorable Member Rajendra Laxmi Gaire, time 7 minutes. (13:41) After this, Honorable Member Samjhana Devkota. Honorable Shri Rajendra Laxmi Gaire (Nepal Communist Party): - Honorable Chairperson, as we are discussing various issues today, at this moment, in our villages, it is the season for Kafal to ripen and be eaten. Birds also chirp, 'Kafal has ripened, Kafal has ripened.' In our villages, people bring Kafals in baskets, go door to door selling them, and at the chauntries... My home is Tansen, Palpa. In Tansen, at the Andolan Chowk, there is a chauntari. If you look at that chauntari, it is never empty of vegetables. The selling of vegetables there is older than us. People sell food, Kafals, sitting at chauntaris, in the shade, around the bus park. Seeing the incident where Kafals were thrown from a woman's basket in Birendranagar, I was reminded of all the chauntaris and roads in our villages. They sell like this in my village too. If they are thrown like this, how will the people in our villages buy notebooks and pens for their children? How will they educate them? I became very worried, and Palpa district is self-sufficient in vegetables, meat, and milk. If we had not allowed such vegetables and fruits to be sold, if we had not promoted them, perhaps we would not be self-sufficient today. Our Palpa district is self-sufficient in that regard. Therefore, such sensitive issues probably occur not only in my district but in all places in the country. Kafals that ripen in Birendranagar probably ripen in the east as well. Why are governments not being sensitive to the public now? This is a concern in my mind. Seeing this irresponsible expression and irresponsible behavior here today, it feels as if the country is facing a disaster. Therefore, I learned only yesterday, on Jestha 11th, that the Health Insurance Board meeting decided to stop the insurance from the 16th. Our Mission Hospital, established in 2011 BS, is in Palpa, it is very old. Not only in Palpa, but many people from neighboring districts and the Terai come there for treatment. Similarly, Lumbini Medical College has served many people. Even I take regular medicine. I have insurance at Lumbini Medical College. I also get it from there. Many people, including chronically ill patients, take medicine regularly. Today, how will this affect the Nepali people if such things are stopped? What will they eat? How will those without money eat? Why are we not being sensitive? I feel so. Similarly, in the health sector, we hear that about 50 industries in Nepal are about to be closed. We hear that tens of thousands of people who were employed will become unemployed today. What are we trying to do? Where are we trying to take this country? Are we building this country or destroying it? Yesterday, for the sake of food, shelter, and clothing for the people, we carried the communist flag in the 2036 BS referendum. We did not care about fire, water, or sun. We endured the police batons and fought for the freedom of the people, risking our lives, and the system we brought here allows people to eat, live, and do business without fear, and to have their rights included. Not only this, we fought for women's rights, indigenous people's rights, the rights of backward regions, proportional representation based on population, inclusion, and involving youth. This is a system we fought for. It is a system we fought for women's rights. Because we brought it with great difficulty, we cherish it greatly. We have added layers upon layers of problems. We have become homeless. If we keep demolishing the houses built with suffering, where will our country go? What are we trying to do? I remember when the political change happened, a DSP named Bhim Dhakal came to our district. At that time, those with unusual hairstyles, called thugs, hooligans, were brought together through consensus, their hair was cut, and they were sent back as respectable citizens. Yesterday, we used to call those who smoked cigarettes, drank tea, and smoked marijuana 'mandales'. Today, that character is found here. Is such a character seen in the parliament too? We are seeing such things. We don't know if this is good or bad. We who fought for the revolution, we considered it unusual and did not consider it good. Perhaps the youth of today consider it good. Their interests and ours are different. Therefore, our Finance Minister has said that this is new, there is something new in this bill. He said that we are not just leaving poverty, but trying to uplift the middle class. If we are bringing something new, then brother, sister, neighbor, friend...

Can we give up what we said? That is our tradition. It is customary to visit neighbors. There is a matter of helping during times of death, isn't there? Our society, our tradition is to help each other build houses. Therefore, how can we preserve good things and discard bad things? For that, we need to join hands and dialogue. The minister should not speak. If they don't speak, then the Prime Minister also won't speak. Then there will be no dialogue between ministers and the Prime Minister. There will be no dialogue between ministers and members of parliament. Even if MPs clash, there will be no dialogue. If this happens, how will we achieve development? Therefore, it is necessary to learn from the past and connect with new technologies. For this, our cooperation is essential. We want to move this country forward through cooperation and dialogue, and we can. Therefore, in the upcoming budget, how can we make the public self-reliant? How can we earn income from agricultural products, herbs, minerals, and natural resources? I conclude by stating that the government should bring this into the budget. (13:49 hrs) Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Samjhana Devkota, time is 10 minutes. After this, Honorable Member Mohammad Khalid. 12 Honorable Ms. Samjhana Devkota (Nepal Communist Party, UML):- Honorable (13:49 hrs) b Chairperson, as I stand here today, I feel somewhat uncomfortable. The members of the House of Representatives are given more importance as people's representatives. The fact that members of the National Assembly are representatives of representatives is somewhat overlooked. I had thought of not speaking today, I had no intention of speaking. But yesterday, the calls from my constituents constantly urged me. I also called local levels in many districts of my province, Gandaki Province. What is happening where you are? Everything else was fine, but the public is evicting local representatives from their offices. Why? I asked. They told me, "Farmers are coming daily with delegations. When will we get fertilizer? When will we apply fertilizer to our crops? The maize and millet have been sown. The monsoon paddy has been planted. The government says that by making us self-reliant in food grains, we can increase production and become self-reliant in food." I want to tell the ministers of the government that after going through many stages, only then does a farmer become a farmer. I thought, a farmer is not respected in the first place. A farmer is considered dirty. They play in the dirt, they play in the mud. We look at them with contempt, like flies or insects working in filth. A country where farmers are not respected can never be respected. I think we need to pay attention to this argument. Also, farmers do not have land. The previous government raised the issue of land, but it was not managed properly. Although it has been included in the policy and program now, I want to say that a policy should be made to provide land as needed. The government should bring programs accordingly. Also, we have not been dependent on anything else so far, but we are dependent on seeds. We are subordinate. Whatever seeds are sent, farmers are forced to sow them. What is the government thinking about quality seeds for correct and quality seeds? We are eager to see what programs the government will bring in that regard. My elder sister, the honorable member, has also spoken about the problems of farmers. I want to draw the government's attention to bringing quality seeds and ensuring that farmers do not have to cry over ruined crops in the future. Also, I am a farmer, my country, my father was also a farmer. I also engage in farming in my free time, but there is no irrigation. Most of the areas, a very large area, depend on rainwater. Therefore, if we want to promote farmers, we need to focus on increasing irrigation and providing irrigation facilities. I want to emphasize again, fertilizer. Although I heard somewhere that fertilizer is being made from AI, and an honorable member spoke about it in the House of Representatives recently. If everything is to be done by AI, let's embrace AI technology. But it might not be just AI. It might be practical matters, it might be various technologies. We may not have that knowledge in this generation. Perhaps young people might have it. We may not have it. But I want fertilizer for the farmers. Farmers have been running for fertilizer for many days, hundreds of days. If they get it, they don't get more than five kilograms. What is five kilograms of fertilizer for? It's not medicine. It's fertilizer. Production doesn't happen without fertilizer. Therefore, the government had ample time to manage fertilizer in a timely manner. We were elected in February. Two to three months is a significant time for us. Why couldn't the government utilize this time? The government might still be working, but this delay will no longer be acceptable to the public. Let's talk about security. We have to protect every plant from insects and pests. Wild animals like monkeys, deer, bears, etc., are destroying crops in the fields. My neighbor, who is almost 79 years old, having passed 75, called me and said, "I am in the field, child. I have made a monkey-proof enclosure with a small net. I cannot leave here until the sun sets." The daily lives of thousands of fathers, mothers, sisters, and brothers are spent like this. Bills are coming in rapidly, but why are there no bills to protect the public like this? Why are laws not being made? I want to draw the government's attention. Similarly, we produce, but the production is high, yet we cannot preserve it sustainably, we cannot store it. Production is high. New technology has increased production, but it is not durable. We cannot preserve it without pesticides. Without proper storage, how to store the produced food grains requires many hurdles for a farmer to survive. Therefore, land for farmers, fertilizer and seeds for farmers, irrigation for farmers, crop protection and storage for farmers, there can be many more such processes. Only after completing these many processes does the farmer's sweat enter the house. Even after entering the house, monkeys are causing trouble inside the house. Just a few days ago, in my village, monkeys entered two or three houses and took away cooked food. The fear of monkeys is not small, the fear of wild animals is not small. The villages are deserted, and in the sparse settlements that remain, the rampant presence of wild animals makes it difficult for life itself to be safe, let alone protecting other animals, domestic animals, and the crops and seeds produced. Therefore, if we want to promote village settlements, village farmers, village land, and village production, we need to discuss how to provide relief to farmers through that means. The government can no longer operate without accountability. We in the National Assembly also deserve time. Do the ministers get time from the Prime Minister? We are eager to see the Prime Minister. Will we even recognize him if we meet him on the street now? I am worried that we might have to address others as Prime Minister. Therefore, I request that the Prime Minister be introduced, and the ministers also be introduced. Who among the ministers is here today? Which ministry are they from? I also want to know this. I am ignorant, I am unaware. Therefore, I request through the Honorable Chairperson to provide me with this facility as well. It seems that our government represents the poor, or not. They seem to have the financial resources to eat gold, relax in gold, sleep on beds of gold, and travel in palaces of gold, but the public is not like that. We are representatives of the helpless public. When we speak, it might be uncomfortable for you. It might be said, "Why is she only talking about the poor?" But I am the child of the poor, the daughter of the poor, the daughter of a farmer. I still have calluses on my hands because I come from that class. Therefore, until the problems of the farmers are heard, until the farmers are respected, until their plight is understood, I cannot be a true representative. Therefore, I want to see not only my constituency, not only my Gandaki Province, but all Nepali farmers smiling. I want to see all Nepali farmers with self-respect. I want an environment to be created where all Nepali people are encouraged to pursue farming. Therefore, in the future, after the National Assembly, it will still be the farmers. Therefore, many of us can live as farmers in the future. We can be a reflection of those farmers. The government can address those farmers. Their difficulties, their fertilizer, seeds, irrigation, land, can be obtained when sought. Therefore, I want to tell the government that if the nation is to prosper, the government must take responsibility for land, health, and education. The government's policies and programs must now move in that direction. We are giving relief to the public, listening to the public's concerns; only when we make these three things accessible will the public be happy. (....Time expired.) Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Mohammad Khalid, time is 5 minutes. (13:59 hrs) After this, Honorable Member Bishnu Kumari Sapkota. Honorable Mr. Mohammad Khalid (People's Socialist Party, Nepal):- Honorable (14:00 hrs) Chairperson, tomorrow is Eid al-Adha, or Bakr Eid. I extend my greetings and best wishes for it. Honorable Chairperson, a new budget is coming. The Nepali people have given unprecedented support and cooperation to this government, and with unprecedented support comes unprecedented expectations. Therefore, I want to present a few points regarding the public's expectations. What is the state of inflation? Currently, it is sky-high, and especially the poor and middle class are unable to live on their income. The Nepali people expect that the government will control inflation through this budget, and it must be reflected in the budget. Petroleum products, what were the statements of the leaders of the current government regarding this in the past? I do not want to recall that. What I want is action. The public is waiting for action. The price is somewhat unnatural; it should be adjusted to provide relief to the public. Similarly, I hope that the trend of youth going abroad will decrease. We want that when the next year's budget or policy and program are introduced, we can congratulate and thank the government. We can say, "Look, this government has worked; this many people were going abroad, now there is a reduction of this much percentage." Such policies must come. Youth are all on social media. How much debt will you increase? The public is watching. What relief will you provide to the exploited and oppressed people? Will you advance development programs based on fair distribution of resources and population? Especially the Madhesi people are watching this very closely. They are waiting to see what will be done. Because only 12/13 of the 53 percent population...

Percentage of budget given so far. If it's new, the Madhesi people are waiting for the new. Considering the growing despair, suicide, lack of irrigation, unemployment etc. in the Madhesh region, it is waiting for a special package. According to state statistics, the Muslim community is the most backward in terms of education, health, employment, income, politics, and access to state mechanisms. This community is also hoping for relief. My wish is that the government be successful, and the budget is also a part of that success. Therefore, the budget must be balanced, just, and in accordance with the spirit of the constitution. When considering and discussing the budget, let us all enthusiastically support and welcome such a budget. With this hope and vision, I would like to take leave. Thank you. Presiding Officer: Honorable Vice-Chairperson Ms. Lila Kumari Bhandari. (14:03) p 97 Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Bishnu Kumari Sapkota, time 11 minutes. After this, Honorable Member Renu Chand. Honorable Ms. Bishnu Kumari Sapkota (Nepali Congress): Honorable Chairperson, isn't the local government one of the three important bodies of the state? Local government is the foundation of all of us. We have all been born and raised in the local government. We have all come this far after being born and raised in local government. Today, to strengthen the federal system, if we are to truly strengthen it, we must strengthen the local government. Today, the representatives of local governments are extremely worried. The grant that local governments will receive to work in the budget being brought by the government, the grant they will receive in the budget, the equalization grant has been cut. For this, the Municipal Association of Nepal, the National Association of Municipalities, and the National Association of Rural Municipalities have held discussions. Their meetings are ongoing. They contacted me. We are also accountable to the local government because they have elected and sent us. Today, even for local governments, when making policies and programs in the first phase of the budget, the government should have called representatives of the associations of rural and municipal municipalities and at least consulted them for suggestions before making policies. That was not done. Even if it was not done, at least when making the budget, the local government, what is it doing? What will this budget do? We should have thought about it, but that could not happen. The Municipal Association and the Rural Municipalities Association are displeased and have expressed objections regarding the cut in grants, and have also held in-depth discussions. Honorable Chairperson, the first beginning of human development is pre-primary education. What attention have we paid to pre-primary education? I want to draw the attention of this government to this. I want to say that attention should be paid to this when allocating the budget. Looking at our history of human development, we have not reached this point just like that. We have come here through great struggle, sacrifice, penance, martyrdom, and contribution. The 104-year Rana regime in our country was not overthrown just like that. Our respected leaders, brave men, great leaders struggled immensely. Even when this government took the step of executing them, they were not afraid for the sake of nationality. Similarly, the condition of Nepali women was even more precarious. We Nepali women were truly stateless. We didn't even have citizenship. We had no rights. We had no right to property, let alone rights to education, health. We didn't have citizenship. We couldn't even contest elections because we didn't have voting rights. From 1997, Nepali women Divya Devi Koirala, Yogmaya Neupane. Yogmaya Neupane, along with 40 other women, committed mass suicide because the government did not listen to their pleas. Yesterday's leaders sacrificed their homes, their property, and struggled immensely for the sake of nationality. In 1997, women's voices were raised. Gradually, in 2003, the women's revolution took place. Along with the great leader of the Nepali Congress, Bishweshwar Prasad Koirala, Suvarna Shamsher, Krishna Prasad Bhattarai, Ganesh Man Singh, Manmohan Adhikari, Pushpalal Shrestha, Girija Prasad Koirala, etc., women were also present at every juncture. Divya Devi Koirala, Mangala Devi Singh, Nona Koirala, Indira Acharya, Shailaja Acharya, Sahana Pradhan, Sadhana Pradhan, and many other women led movements. In 2004, under the leadership of Mangala Devi Singh, the founding president of the Nepal Women's Association, we Nepali women obtained citizenship. Today, we have not looked back at that history. The movement was carried out in such a way that no one would be hurt, not a single small hut in the country would be destroyed, not a single twig would be broken. King Mahendra built all those roads, and they are still walking on them, kicking up dust. How many roads did Mahendra build? Today, there is no village without a motorable road. Today, when this government went to the villages to ask for votes, it was probably easy for them to travel on those roads. Today, forgetting that, the government has insulted the old regime by calling it the old power, this should not be done. To establish this tomorrow morning as well, by advancing the work done yesterday, and in the coming days, the upcoming budget will not build anything, will not draw any development plans. Today, from smart mobiles to everything digital, roads, paths, mines, water, buildings, everything is there. Health, education, everything has been built, but it just needs to be managed. For managing it, without any hesitation, keeping in mind the gender-responsive budget, let's move forward. Thank you, Jai Nepal. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Renu Chand, time 8 minutes. After this, Honorable Member Meena Singh Rakhal. Displaced people have been housed in holding centers in Ichadu, Kirtipur, Bode, Nagarkot, Bhaktapur, Banepa, and some hotels and lodges. The condition of the holding centers is bad, terrible. An example of this is when displaced children go to schools in new places, forgive me, Chairperson, to use this word, children, when children of the landless come, they are ridiculed. Even when children say they will not go to schools in such an environment, they are looked down upon, saying these are children of the landless, they are like this, where will they study, they are thieves, robbers, gangsters. The structures of projects including ADB are being rapidly built in the place where they were displaced. Honorable Chairperson, I seek permission to express my views on a contemporary issue. The country is currently going through a serious and difficult situation. In this situation, the responsibility, duty, and dignity of this respected assembly, the National Assembly, are even more significant.

We are terrified that the current government's planned attacks on the leadership of political parties, universities and academic heritages, the private sector, landless squatters, laborers, and the judiciary might destroy our established history, culture, customs, and traditions with this kind of retaliatory, angry, and whimsical governance.

I will connect this to a folk tale. I want to present a folk tale here. I don't know if I will be able to finish it. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Shri Krishna Prasad Adhikari, time 10 minutes. (2:39 PM) Honorable Shri Krishna Prasad Adhikari (Nepal Communist Party):- (2:40 PM) Honorable Chairperson, today I seek permission to express my views on the problems of the landless. For the past one month, the government, by mobilizing a large number of security forces, army, and police, has bulldozed settlements of landless, Dalits, squatters, and unorganized residents who have been living in various parts of the country, including the Kathmandu Valley, for decades, causing damage to physical property worth billions. The government has committed a serious violation of human rights by forcibly evicting squatters in an inhumane manner. The interim order of the respected court to stop the forced eviction of landless squatters without identifying them and providing alternative arrangements is also being ignored, and a bulldozer terror is ongoing in various parts of the country, including Kohalpur. The Ministry of Home Affairs has sent letters to all 77 districts to vacate the shacks of squatters. Letters have been sent to 753 local levels. Currently, the government has provided data that 2,616 households displaced in the Kathmandu Valley, comprising 11,001 individuals, have been housed in holding centers such as hotels, lodges, ashrams, stadiums, vocational training centers, and the Red Cross. During the on-site observation of the holding centers by the National Assembly's Public Policy and Delegated Legislation Committee and the Federalism Strengthening and National Concerns Committee, the situation observed in the holding centers was dire. Displaced individuals are crammed into small rooms. Members of the same family cannot stay together. There is no proper arrangement for clean drinking water, toilets, and sanitation. The arrangement for health check-ups and medicines is not good. In some places, water mixed with sewage is being supplied. There is no proper arrangement for regular health check-ups and medical treatment for chronically ill patients, pregnant women, the elderly, mothers who have just given birth, and children. There is no arrangement for nutritious food in the morning and evening, or adequate clothing. The education of children has been disrupted due to their absence from school. The work of daily wage laborers has stopped. Permission is required to go in and out. Most of the women, men, and children staying in the holding centers feel like they are living a prisoner's life in a detention center. Two people have committed suicide. The media is being prevented from taking photos and broadcasting from there. Honorable Chairperson, the landless, squatters, Dalits, and marginalized people of Nepal have a long history of struggling repeatedly for housing and land. Currently, more than 1.2 million landless, squatters, Dalits, and unorganized residents are protesting nationwide. In the past, the autocratic Panchayat system and the monarchy set fire to the settlements of landless squatters and Dalits, trampled them with elephants, and brutally suppressed and drove them away with boots, sticks, and bullets. Today, it appears that the government is using the boots of the army and police to trample, and bulldozers to drive away, the settlements of landless squatters, Dalits, and unorganized residents. Is the government not looking for excuses to evade its constitutional responsibility to ensure the land rights of millions of landless, Dalit, squatter, and unorganized resident families across the country? A question has arisen: is the government trying to remove them from the holding centers by giving them Rs. 14,000 per month and pushing back their land rights for years? Article 37 of the Constitution, under the Right to Housing, states in Sub-section 1 that every citizen has the right to adequate housing, and in Sub-section 2, no citizen shall be evicted or encroached upon their owned residence except as provided by law. Article 40, concerning the Rights of Dalits, states in Sub-section 5 that the state shall provide land to landless Dalits once as per law, and in Sub-section 6, the state shall arrange for housing for homeless Dalits as per law. Article 42 of the Constitution, concerning the Right to Social Justice, states in Sub-section 4 that every farmer shall have access to land for agricultural work as per law. Under Part 4, Directive Principles, Policies, and Responsibilities of the State, Section 'D' deals with policies related to agriculture and land reform. Sub-section 'Chha' of the policy on social justice and inclusion mentions the identification of freed Kamaiyas, Kamalari, and squatters for settlement. Haruwa, Charuwa, Haliya, and landless are the main ones. The government is trying to evade its responsibility to protect citizens and its duty to the state by not fulfilling the rights stipulated by the constitution. Why is the government so eager to curb the fundamental rights of the citizens? I want to state that Prime Minister Balen Shah should answer this house. According to the criteria of the Federal Commission for the Management of Alternative Housing, evicting anyone forcibly without prior notice, community consultation, arrangement of alternative housing, resettlement and compensation, continuity of education and health services, and opportunity for legal remedy is a serious violation of human rights. Other countries' experiences show that America has tried to solve the landless problem through housing assistance, India through judicial and land reform, and South Asian countries through resettlement and community housing. The world's experience shows that a policy of forceful eviction without management is completely wrong. Resettlement, linked with housing, education, health, employment, social justice, and economic opportunities, is the path to a long-term, sustainable, and just solution. In Nepal, the government has weakened the constitutional values, human rights, democracy, and humanitarian principles by evicting squatters, Dalits, and unorganized residents without preparing for alternative management and resettlement. Honorable Chairperson, according to the data of the Land Commission, 1,220,194 families have submitted applications. I want to state that the government should study this problem thoroughly and make arrangements for a permanent solution for the truly landless who do not own land anywhere in the country. Similarly, those whose houses and land have been washed away by floods, those who have houses in their ancestral property but no land in practice, and such people who have come to the city and are living as laborers by setting up a small shelter for years. I want to state that the government should also prioritize scientific research, scientific testing, and surveying of these issues. I want to request the government to collect data on all types of land lost due to Guthi land and river course changes, manage the land scientifically, provide dignified residential land to the actual landless for a permanent solution, turn the holding centers into facilities and residential resettlement centers, arrange compensation for the physical damage suffered by the displaced families, establish resettlement centers on a fast track for areas that need to be cleared from riverbanks, riverbeds, and landslide-prone areas, and connect the resettlement centers and housing with daily livelihoods by making adequate provisions in the budget for education, health, skills, training, social security, transportation, schools, health posts, drinking water, internet, markets, and employment. Finally, I want to say that the squatters are currently suffering and struggling in a pathetic and painful situation, and the government should not lose its composure. The government should not act hastily and regret it later, and it should not take the problems of the squatters lightly. Thank you. Presiding Officer: Honorable Chairperson Shri Narayan Prasad Dahal. With the permission of the Chairperson, I will inform the assembly in accordance with Rule 124, Sub-rule one of the National Assembly Regulations, 2075. (a) Mr. Secretary, National Assembly, Subject: Bill sent with message. It is requested that the 'Bill to Amend the Election of Members of the House of Representatives, 2083', originating in the House of Representatives, was passed by the House of Representatives on Tuesday, Jestha 12, 2083, in its presented form without amendment, and therefore, in accordance with Rule 127, Sub-rule one of the House of Representatives Regulations, 2079, the said bill is sent with a message. Prakash Adhikari, Secretary, Jestha 13, 2083. (b) Mr. Secretary, National Assembly, Subject: Bill sent with message. It is requested that the 'Bill to Amend the Voter Roll, 2083', originating in the House of Representatives, was passed by the House of Representatives on Tuesday, Jestha 12, 2083, in its presented form without amendment, and therefore, in accordance with Rule 127, Sub-rule one of the House of Representatives Regulations, 2079, the said bill is sent with a message. Prakash Adhikari, Secretary, Jestha 13, 2083. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable members, the next meeting of the National Assembly will be held today, Jestha 13, 2083, Wednesday, at 3:10 PM, i.e., after 10 minutes. This meeting is adjourned. (Thereafter, the next meeting was adjourned to be held today, Jestha 13, 2083, Wednesday, at 3:10 PM, i.e., after 10 minutes.) Adjourned: 14:00.

sections.name: Opening
sections.summary_en: The National Assembly meeting commenced at 13:19 hours under the chairmanship of Honourable Chairperson Narayan Prasad Dahal. The Chairperson announced the commencement of proceedings and the allocation of time for Zero Hour.

speakers.name: Narayan Prasad Dahal
speakers.topic: Opening of session and Zero Hour announcement

sections.name: Zero Hour
sections.summary_en: During Zero Hour, Honourable Member Chandra Bahadur KC raised the issue of wildlife-related damages in 16 districts and proposed a solar fence system. Honourable Member Jagat Timilsina highlighted the ongoing protest by professors and staff at Tribhuvan University due to lack of government attention. Honourable Member Ranjit Karna demanded the revocation of the suspension of the health insurance program and scientific management of rural settlements affected by disasters. Honourable Member Rekha Kumari Jha expressed concern over rising crime rates in the Terai region and called for increased border surveillance and youth programs. Honourable Member Roshi Mechhe criticized the federal government's approach to removing squatters without providing alternatives, citing the constitutional right to housing. Honourable Member Samjhana Devkota questioned the government's lack of response to issues raised in Zero Hour and Special Time. Honourable Member Somnath Poudel demanded action against an insurance company for failing to compensate farmers for banana crop damage due to storms and called for government relief.

sections.name: Special Time
sections.summary_en: During Special Time, Honourable Member Kamala Panta criticized the Prime Minister's disregard for parliament, questioned the President's actions regarding the policy and program, and demanded government accountability and answers to issues raised by MPs. She also emphasized the importance of the rule of law and constitutional adherence. She further raised concerns about the right to housing for squatters and the need for proper management before displacement, and the issue of capital flight and facilitating businesses.

speakers.name: Kamala Panta
speakers.topic: PM's disregard for parliament, President's actions, rule of law, squatters, capital flight

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker criticizes the government's economic policies, highlighting issues like capital flight, lack of dialogue with political parties, and the impact of rising prices on the poor. They emphasize the need for government accountability and inclusive policies.

speakers.topic: Government accountability and economic policies

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker expresses concern over the government's anti-poor stance, citing increased prices of essentials and lack of support for farmers. They question the government's policies and the effectiveness of the 100-day program, noting employee fear and rising public transport fares.

speakers.topic: Government's anti-poor policies and economic issues

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker discusses the plight of farmers, questioning the low prices for their produce like milk and potatoes. They urge the government to support production and express concern about the upcoming paddy season facing fertilizer shortages.

speakers.topic: Farmer issues and agricultural production

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker highlights the challenges faced by rural communities due to wildlife like monkeys, tigers, and wild boars destroying crops and livestock. They question the government's programs to address these issues and provide relief to the public.

speakers.topic: Wildlife menace and rural challenges

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker criticizes the government's plan to abolish the Drinking Water Corporation, questioning the lack of alternative solutions and the potential impact on water supply projects. They also express concern about the government's haste in implementing policies and its handling of landless issues.

speakers.topic: Abolition of Drinking Water Corporation and policy implementation

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker questions the government's move to abolish trade unions, stating it contradicts constitutional rights. They argue that any such change requires a constitutional amendment and that actions must be in line with the constitution.

speakers.topic: Trade unions and constitutional rights

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Honorable Member Rajendra Laxmi Gaire speaks about the tradition of selling Kafal in villages and the impact of incidents like the one in Birendranagar on rural livelihoods. She highlights Palpa's self-sufficiency in agricultural produce and questions the government's sensitivity towards public issues.

speakers.name: Rajendra Laxmi Gaire
speakers.topic: Rural livelihoods and government insensitivity

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker expresses concern over the decision to stop health insurance from Jestha 16th, highlighting the impact on patients relying on institutions like Mission Hospital and Lumbini Medical College. They also mention the potential closure of industries and resulting unemployment.

speakers.name: Rajendra Laxmi Gaire
speakers.topic: Health insurance and economic impact

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker reflects on the struggles for rights and the current system, questioning the direction of the country. They recall the fight for basic needs and rights like women's and indigenous people's rights, and express concern about the demolition of established structures.

speakers.name: Rajendra Laxmi Gaire
speakers.topic: Reflection on past struggles and current direction

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker contrasts past revolutionary ideals with current trends, questioning the acceptance of certain behaviors. They mention the Finance Minister's statement about uplifting the middle class and express a desire for inclusive policies.

speakers.name: Rajendra Laxmi Gaire
speakers.topic: Revolutionary ideals and current trends

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: A member discusses the importance of preserving good traditions and fostering dialogue between the public and government officials. They emphasize the need for self-reliance through agriculture and natural resources in the upcoming budget. Another member highlights the challenges faced by farmers, including lack of fertilizer, irrigation, and protection from wildlife, and calls for government action to address these issues.

speakers.name: Honorable Member Samjhana Devkota
speakers.topic: Farmers' issues, agricultural support, and government accountability

speakers.name: Honorable Member Mohammad Khalid
speakers.topic: Inflation, petroleum prices, youth employment, and budget expectations

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Honorable Member Bishnu Kumari Sapkota raised concerns about the budget's impact on local governments, highlighting cuts in equalization grants and the lack of consultation with local bodies. She also emphasized the need for attention to pre-primary education and the historical struggles of Nepali women. Honorable Member Renu Chand criticized the government's actions regarding the landless, detailing forced evictions, poor conditions in holding centers, and the government's perceived bias towards the upper class.

speakers.name: Bishnu Kumari Sapkota
speakers.topic: Budget, local government, pre-primary education, women's rights

speakers.name: Renu Chand
speakers.topic: Landless evictions, holding centers, government bias

key_issues: Historical struggles of women in Nepal

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: A member raised concerns about the government's actions regarding landless people, alleging violations of constitutional rights and laws. The member demanded documents related to displacement decisions and criticized the government's approach as arbitrary and inhumane. Another member highlighted a tragic bus accident in Kapilvastu, urging for free treatment for the injured, investigation, and improved road safety. They also criticized the frequent power outages in Karnali Province and the government's failure to provide reliable electricity.

speakers.name: Minar Singh Rakhal
speakers.topic: Government actions, constitutional rights, displacement, bus accident, power outages

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: A member expressed condolences for martyrs and criticized the government's perceived attacks on political leadership, academia, the private sector, and the judiciary, calling it retaliatory and whimsical. The member highlighted the fear and uncertainty in the private sector due to government actions and the lack of adherence to legal principles. Concerns were also raised about the government's approach towards landless squatters, laborers, and vulnerable communities, describing it as inhumane. The member also criticized the attacks on the judiciary and universities.

speakers.name: Jagat Timilsina
speakers.topic: Government's actions against institutions, private sector, landless, judiciary, universities

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: A member criticizes the government's handling of university appointments and the overall state of higher education, alleging corruption and lack of meritocracy. Another member raises concerns about the government's eviction of landless squatters, highlighting human rights violations and inadequate living conditions in holding centers, and calls for adherence to constitutional rights.

speakers.name: Shri Krishna Prasad Adhikari
speakers.topic: Landless squatters' rights and government evictions

sections.name: Special Time
sections.summary_en: Honorable Member Shri Krishna Prasad Adhikari speaks about the problems of landless squatters, detailing the government's actions of eviction, the poor conditions in holding centers, and the violation of their rights. He references constitutional provisions and international experiences in addressing landless issues.

speakers.name: Shri Krishna Prasad Adhikari
speakers.topic: Landless squatters' rights and government evictions

sections.name: Adjournment
sections.summary_en: The Chairperson announces the conclusion of the special time for members' speeches and schedules the presentation of the Economic Survey for the fiscal year 2082/083 by the Finance Minister.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The Finance Minister presents the Economic Survey for the fiscal year 2082/083, highlighting global economic uncertainties and projecting Nepal's economic growth, GDP size, per capita income, and sectoral contributions.

speakers.name: Dr. Swarnim Wagle
speakers.topic: Presentation of Economic Survey 2082/083

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The Economic Survey 2082/083 was presented, highlighting economic indicators such as inflation, revenue, expenditure, public debt, trade balance, remittances, foreign exchange reserves, and digital payments. It also covered agricultural production, foreign investment, electricity access, road infrastructure, tourism, human development indicators, health insurance, social security, drinking water access, carbon trading, and Sustainable Development Goals. While acknowledging satisfactory progress in some areas, the survey noted persistent challenges like low economic growth, sluggish credit flow, and widening trade deficit.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The Secretary of the National Assembly informed the assembly about messages received from the House of Representatives concerning two amendment bills: the 'Bill to Amend the Election of Members of the House of Representatives, 2083' and the 'Bill to Amend the Voter Roll, 2083'. Both bills were passed by the House of Representatives without amendment.

speakers.name: Tul Bahadur Kandel
speakers.topic: Informing about messages from House of Representatives on bills

bills_discussed.name: Bill to Amend the Election of Members of the House of Representatives, 2083
Bill to Amend the Voter Roll, 2083

key_issues: Election of Members of the House of Representatives Amendment Bill

sections.name: Adjournment
sections.summary_en: The Chairperson announced that the National Assembly would reconvene after a short break of 10 minutes, with the next meeting scheduled for 3:10 PM on Jestha 13, 2083.
